title: Rejoicing
hookLine: a friend posts the win you wanted; Shantideva opens chapter three by being glad for everyone
tomorrow: he wishes he were something you swallow. what is it?

lines: GLAD FOR SOMEONE WHO BEAT YOU?
cards: The group chat lights up. A friend got the thing you both applied for: the spot, the part, the prize. There's a photo.
Everyone's sending hearts. Your thumb hovers over the keyboard, and what comes up first isn't joy. It's a small, hot question: why her?
So, yesterday's question, asked straight: can you be glad for someone who just beat you? Shantideva starts chapter three by trying, on purpose, with everyone.
And inside Buddhism there's more than one view of how honest that is.

teach.b: First voice: Shantideva. Chapter three opens with him rejoicing, gladly, in the good done by all beings, the good that eases their suffering.
He rejoices in those set free, in the bodhisattvas' long road, in the Buddhas' awakening. The word is anumodana, rejoicing in someone else's good.
His best case: rejoicing is a practice, not a mood. You do it before you feel it, the way you stretch before you're flexible, and envy loosens.
And it judges the deed, not the doer: a hungry person who got fed is fed, whoever posted the photo.

teach.h: THE OTHER VOICE: INTENTION IS THE ACT.
teach.b: Second voice, which leans on the Buddha's own words in the Pali suttas: intention, he says, is what makes an act what it is. So a good deed done to be seen is mixed.
Its best case: honest people shouldn't cheer vanity as if it were pure, and saying congratulations you don't feel can turn into a habit of saying things you don't mean.
Where they meet: Shantideva never claims motives don't matter, and the second voice never says don't be glad. One says start with the gladness.

teach.h: START GLAD, AND KEEP IT HONEST.
teach.b: The other says keep it honest.

how: In Theravada temples, people answer a good deed or a shared blessing with sadhu, sadhu, sadhu, an expression of rejoicing; in Mahayana practice, rejoicing in others' good is one of the regular steps of a daily liturgy.

o: being glad for the good someone else has done
a festival held when the temple's harvest comes in
celebrating loudly so that others can see your joy

games.q: two voices on rejoicing — tap the pairs.
p: a practice, not a mood: start glad
intention is what makes the act
start glad, and keep it honest

s: you should only rejoice once you truly feel happy for someone
Shantideva treats rejoicing as a practice you begin before the feeling, the way you stretch before you're flexible.
the Pali suttas say intention is what makes an act what it is
that's the root of the second voice: a deed done to be seen is mixed.
the two views disagree about whether to be glad at all
neither says don't be glad. one starts with gladness; the other keeps it honest.

games.q: a classmate posts photos of herself volunteering, clearly for the likes. a friend says rejoicing in it would be fake. what's the fairest version of your friend's view?
o: intention shapes the act, so cheering a show as pure would be dishonest.
volunteering for likes does no good at all, so there's nothing to rejoice in.
rejoicing is for monks; ordinary people should just mind their own business.
games.why: that's the second voice at its best. Shantideva's reply: the people she helped were still helped, so rejoice in that good, without praising the show.

practice: Count three good things other people did recently, one on each finger: a kindness you saw, something a friend pulled off, a stranger who held a door.
Pause on each one and let yourself be glad it happened, even if you had no part in it.

wordCard.voice: Rejoicing: being glad for the good someone else did. Shantideva treats it as a practice you start before the feeling arrives.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: rejoicing in, approving of someone else's good. Chapter three opens with it.

carryVoice: The line for today: glad for all, starting with the one who beat you. Chapter three, begun.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 3.1-3.4 (rejoicing in the good of all beings, in liberation, in the bodhisattvas and the Buddhas)
Anguttara Nikaya 6.63 (Nibbedhika Sutta: intention is kamma)
